text:
Candriani was not listening to her; drunk with joy, now able to gaze at her with all the intensity of a desire no longer restrained, he gazed avidly over her whole body, from her head to her little feet, whose tips peeped out from beneath the very hem of her skirt.

“I shall make you forget Filippo,” he said suddenly. “You will no longer love him; I am free and alone, I can devote my entire life to you.... Love him still today, it does not matter; it is right that you should love him; it will be for me to erase his image from your heart.”

And all at once he burst out:

“I am happy; I am happy to see you here beside me; you remembered that I offered you my friendship in a desperate situation, and that consoles me for many sorrows.... Ah, I assure you, Loredana, that I am no longer the thoughtless man you once knew! I love you tenderly and hope that I may reassure you....”

She cut off his words with a gesture.

“No,” she replied. “I shall never love you.”

She looked around, and, seeing the goblet, raised it to lips that she felt were parched by an inward fever.

“Listen to me,” she continued imperiously. “I am here not because I love you, not because I believe in your friendship, but because I wish and must ruin myself.”

“Loredana, Loredana, for pity’s sake!” Berto interrupted.

“I must ruin myself. He is about to commit a crime. His sick mother has asked him to leave me, and he has refused.... No, I cannot accept this sacrifice; it is a horrible thing; I must leave him, and in such a way that he will no longer seek me, no longer desire me.... I do not wish to hurt his mother, who has already suffered so much because of me.... If she were to die—ah, if she were to die—what remorse, what shame!... And one day he would awaken from this madness; and between him and me, always, always, I would see his mother’s corpse.... I must prevent him from dishonoring himself!”

Berto, standing upright, listened with a sense of wonder to the young woman, who spoke rapidly, agitated by violent excitement; her initial pallor had given way to a feverish flush that crimsoned her cheeks, made her eyes shine intensely, and reddened her lips, giving them the color of living blood.

She pleased him so much thus stretched out in the armchair and sunk into the white fur that Berto bent down once more to kiss her hands. Loredana pushed him away.

“I wanted to kill myself,” she continued, “but it would have caused a fresh scandal; they might have accused Filippo of my death.... Ah, how malicious everyone is!... I have been told to my face that I am your mistress, that my honesty is worth nothing because no one believes me, that a man is a thief when everyone calls him a thief.... How many dreadful things I have learned! And then I thought that they were right. The only person who did not doubt me was Filippo; he believes in my love and in my honesty, which everyone laughs at; and so he too must cease to believe, in order that he may be saved.... I thought that, since they call me your mistress, every effort is useless, and I shall never be able to free myself from this accusation....”

“Do not speak so,” Berto interrupted. “It does thee too much harm....”

She stared at him with wide-open eyes; that “thee” seemed to her more brutal than a kiss that had suddenly closed her mouth; but Berto noticed it and added:

“I beg your pardon; I did not mean to offend you. I love you, and I was unable to master myself.”

“No,” said Loredana, rising, “let me go!”

Berto dared to lay a hand on her.

“I beg you,” he murmured, “stay a little longer.....”

Loredana shuddered; gathering up the fur, she searched for her hat with her eyes. But just as she was about to take it up again, she stopped, as though struck by a thought.

Where was she going? To her own home? Filippo would take her back. To Filippo’s home? His mother would die of it. And by then Filippo must already have read the few lines Loredana had left him: “I shall never forget thee; I shall always love thee; the farther away I may seem to thee, the more wholly thine I shall be....” And after this, was she to return to him, with bowed head, like a repentant schoolgirl, and forever too late to be forgiven?

Once more she saw that accursed woman with goatlike feet, half-naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side saw Berto, who dared not move for fear of detaining her, dared not speak for fear of frightening her, and kept watching her, seeking to divine from her gestures the decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and said not a word.

There followed in this manner an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at one another, motionless, almost as though searching each other’s souls; but Berto could endure it no longer, approached her again, and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I implore thee! I know that thou dost not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed and unbuttoned it with a swift gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away, almost in disgust.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the goblet and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour more, and drank once more; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she threw the empty goblet to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you wish to do with me?” she then said.

“Anything thou commandest me,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave this very day, tonight, tomorrow, whenever thou askest it of me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She gave such a harsh and sardonic laugh that Berto looked at her in alarm.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another, it matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I wish to trample upon my entire past, I wish to destroy every memory, I wish nothing to remain, nothing at all, of what was so dear to me and would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think of nothing but taking possession of me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand holding the young woman’s hand loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.
